clauses.text: Every number is one of three types: integer (a whole number from -32768 to 32767), single precision (a real number carrying about 7 significant decimal digits, magnitude up to roughly 1.70141E+38), or double precision (a real number carrying about 16 significant decimal digits, magnitude up to roughly 1.701411834604692E+38). HOW A WRITTEN CONSTANT TAKES ITS TYPE is decided by its notation, not by a single default, and the manual classifies the forms explicitly. Printed p.13 SS5.5 gives the single-precision forms: a real of SEVEN DIGITS OR FEWER, a number carrying a trailing "!", and the exponent form using "E". Printed p.14 SS5.6 gives the double-precision forms: a real of EIGHT DIGITS OR MORE, a number carrying a trailing "#", and the exponent form using "D" -- its own examples being 1234567.890, 56789.0# and -1.09432D-58. So the digit count alone can make an unsuffixed constant double: 1234567 is single and 12345678 is double, with nothing else written differently. A variable with no suffix and no letter-range DEFxxx declaration in effect is single precision by default (printed p.14 SS6.2); that default governs VARIABLES, and a written constant is typed by the rules above. This has a visible consequence that reads as a bug until the two pages are put side by side, and which is worth stating here because it has been reported as one: PRINT 1000000 gives 1E+06 while PRINT 10000000 gives 10000000. The larger number is displayed in full and the smaller in exponent form, because the first is a seven-digit single whose six-digit display budget it exceeds, and the second is an eight-digit double whose budget is sixteen. The display rule (NUM.DISPLAY) is applied consistently; what changes between them is the constant's type.

A variable name, array name, or numeric literal may end in one type-declaration character: % fixes integer, ! fixes single precision, # fixes double precision (a fourth, $, fixes the unrelated string type). The character distinguishes otherwise-identical names -- A, A%, A!, A# and A$ are five separate variables, except that a bare A and an explicit A! name the same one, since single precision is the unsuffixed default. Where no suffix is given, DEFINT/DEFSNG/DEFDBL/DEFSTR set what a name defaults to instead (see PROG.DEFINT and its siblings); an explicit suffix always overrides whatever DEFxxx would otherwise give that name.

Assigning a value to a variable of a different numeric type converts it to the variable's own type: a real assigned to an integer variable rounds to the nearest whole number (ties away from zero), and a value assigned to a lower-precision variable than it came from loses whatever digits that type cannot hold. When two operands of different precision meet in one arithmetic expression, the less precise one converts to match the more precise one before the operation runs, so the result carries the higher of the two types -- except division, which this interpreter also always widens to at least single precision even for two integer operands, since the manual's own operator table describes "/" itself as real-number division, distinct from the integer-division operator this interpreter does not implement. A logical operation (AND, OR, NOT) converts every operand to integer and produces an integer result.

When an assignment or an arithmetic result cannot be represented in its target type's range, this interpreter raises Overflow (OV) and the statement does not complete. The manual's own worked example shows this for assigning an out-of-range real to an integer variable, and CINT and CSNG state the identical bound and outcome for their own conversions to integer and single precision respectively; this interpreter applies the same outcome to every numeric construction uniformly -- a literal, an assignment, or an ordinary arithmetic result exceeding its type's bound all raise Overflow the same way, extending the manual's assignment- and conversion-specific examples to arithmetic in general, which is this interpreter's own reading rather than a case the manual's examples cover directly.

Dividing by zero (or raising zero to a negative power) does not stop the program: the manual states that it prints a short "/0" (Division by zero) notice and continues, substituting the largest number the result's type can represent, with the sign the true result would have had, as the expression's value. DIVERGENT: this interpreter still raises Division by zero as an ordinary halting error instead -- caught by ON ERROR GOTO if one is installed, otherwise stopping the program, the same as every other runtime error here and the same as this interpreter did before this task. Implementing the manual's print-and-continue behaviour is a materially different feature (the evaluator would need to produce output mid-expression, independent of whichever statement is running, and interact with whatever ON ERROR machinery is active) and is left for a future task rather than folded into the type system this task is about.

PRINT always follows a printed number with one space, and reserves one column before it for a sign -- blank for zero or positive, "-" for negative. Single precision prints in ordinary fixed-point form when it fits within 6 significant digits without losing precision, and switches to exponent form (a mantissa, "E", a sign, and the exponent) otherwise; double precision follows the identical rule at 16 significant digits, with "D" in place of "E" as the exponent letter. No type-declaration character is ever appended to printed output. Integer values print as plain whole numbers and never switch to exponent form, since the entire integer range is far short of needing it. The manual does not state the exact magnitude below which a fixed-point value gives way to scientific notation for a very small number; this interpreter uses 0.01 for both single and double precision, carried over unchanged from this codebase's pre-existing behaviour -- a decision of ours, not a manual rule. The small-magnitude boundary is this interpreter's own. Printed p.125 states only that a value showable within the digit budget without losing precision appears in ordinary decimal form; it names no floor, so the floor below which even an in-budget fixed form gives way to exponent form is this interpreter's own. It used to be tested as "the stored float is at least 0.01", which misfired at its own edge: a listing writing .01 gets the single-precision value 0.00999999977, which is NOT at least 0.01, so PRINT .01 produced "1E-02" where ".01" is required under any reading of the page -- one significant digit and two digit characters, well inside a budget of six. The boundary is now read off the RENDERED digits (how many zeros stand between the point and the first significant digit), which is the same boundary and cannot round below a literal written in decimal. A test now pins that specific input.

! fixes a variable name, array name, or numeric literal as single precision. Appended to a variable or array name it declares that name's type outright, overriding any DEFxxx declaration in effect for its first letter; appended to a numeric literal (e.g. 3.14!) it is one of three ways a literal can be written as single precision, alongside a plain real number of 7 digits or fewer and E exponent notation.

# fixes a variable name, array name, or numeric literal as double precision, the same way ! fixes single precision (see NUM.SUFFIX-SINGLE). Appended to a numeric literal (e.g. 56789.0#) it is one of three ways a literal can be written as double precision, alongside a plain real number of 8 digits or more and D exponent notation.

% fixes a variable name, array name, or numeric literal as integer. Appended to a real numeric literal (e.g. 31100.5%) it rounds the literal to the nearest whole number (ties away from zero) where it is written, the same rounding an assignment to an integer variable performs.

An integer constant may be written in one of three notations. The decimal form is the ordinary one. The hexadecimal form is a run of the digits 0 to F introduced by &H, over the range &H0 to &HFFFF. The octal form is a run of the digits 0 to 7 introduced by &O -- or by a bare &, which the manual gives as an equal alternative, so &12345 is an octal constant and not a decimal number carrying a stray sigil -- over the range &0 to &177777. Both ranges are exactly sixteen bits wide. Those sixteen bits are read as a signed integer, so &HFFFF and &177777 are both -1: the manual does not say that outright, but it calls these integer constants, gives ranges reaching 65535, and defines the integer type as -32768 to 32767, and reading the bit pattern as signed is what makes those three statements consistent -- the deduction is ours, not a stated rule. A value written in either non-decimal form is an ordinary integer constant wherever one may appear, and PRINT and the other output statements show it in decimal; HEX$ and OCT$ are what put a value back into its own notation, as strings.

An apostrophe (') may be used in place of REM to introduce a comment. It is the same construct under a shorter name and carries REM's rules with it, including that a colon after the comment text does not end it (see PROG.REM). OPEN QUESTION, recorded 2026-08-28 and not yet settled against the page: this interpreter accepts an apostrophe only where a statement could begin -- at the start of a line, or after a colon -- and REJECTS one that follows a statement directly, so `10 PRINT 1 ' note` is a syntax error while `10 PRINT 1 : ' note` is accepted. In the wider BASIC family the apostrophe's whole advantage over REM is that it needs no separator, which makes the current behaviour suspect, but printed p.135 has not been re-read to confirm what this dialect allows and the scan is not in this repository. The conformance case pins only the line-initial form, so the suite is green and silent on the trailing one. Do not 'fix' this without reading the page: a change here would be a guess wearing a citation.

LINE's ,B option draws a box instead of a single segment: it treats the statement's two endpoints as opposite corners of a rectangle and draws just its four-sided outline, rather than one segment between them. It takes the same optional leading palette-number argument as plain LINE, defaulting to the current graphics foreground colour when left out, and -- unlike ,BF, which the manual states cannot take one at all -- the same optional trailing line-style code plain LINE accepts, dashing the outline. See GFX.LINE for the style's own rules and for the two readings of it that are ours.

LINE's ,BF option means Box Fill: it takes the statement's two endpoints as opposite corners of a rectangle, as ,B does, and fills the rectangle's interior rather than drawing only its outline. Two further arguments belong to BF alone and are meaningless without it: a second palette number giving the colour the interior is filled with, and a tile string giving the pattern it is filled with. When BF is written and both are left out, the interior is filled in the same colour the rectangle was drawn in. Unlike plain LINE and ,B, BF may not be given a line style, which is what lets the one trailing slot be read as a fill here and as a style there. A tile string names the pattern an area is filled with instead of a flat colour, and its meaning is defined once, under [2] PAINT (printed p.118-119 / PDF p.129-130) -- CIRCLE's and LINE's entries only refer to it. A tile is always 8 dots wide, and as many rows tall as the string describes: one character makes a row in monochrome mode, three in the 8-colour mode this interpreter targets, four in 16-colour mode. In colour mode the three characters of a row are bit planes rather than three rows -- for each of the eight dot columns the three bits are read downward as a binary number, and that number is the dot's palette, the first character being the 2^0 plane and bit 7 of each byte the leftmost dot. Characters left over at the end of the string, when its length is not a whole number of rows, are ignored; a string too short for even one row is Illegal function call. Where the pattern is anchored is not addressed by the manual: this interpreter repeats it from the screen origin rather than from where a fill starts, so two adjacent fills of one pattern line up, and that reading is ours.

ABS(<numeric expression>) is the absolute value of the expression. Its result type does not follow its argument's: the manual states the same rule here that it states for SIN and SQR -- the result is double precision when the expression contains a double-precision real, and single precision in every other case, including when the argument is an integer. That rule is observable rather than bookkeeping, since the absolute value of the most negative integer does not fit the integer type: ABS of an integer variable holding -32768 is 32768, where a result that kept the argument's type would raise Overflow instead.

ASC(s) returns the character code of the first character of s, as a decimal integer. The manual does not say what ASC does when s is the null string; this interpreter raises Illegal function call there, the same domain error every other string function in this library raises for an argument outside what it can accept -- a decision of ours, not a rule the manual states.

ATN(n) returns the arctangent of n in radians, in the open range -pi/2 to pi/2. The manual states the result is double precision only when n itself carries a double-precision value, and single precision otherwise, even when n is an integer -- implemented here by tagging the result Double when n's own type is Double, Single otherwise (spec/spec.md NUM.COERCION's typed-value model).

CDBL(n) returns n converted to double precision. Conversion changes only the value's representation, not its precision: the result carries no more significant digits than n's own type already did -- an integer's result has no fractional part beyond n's own whole value, and a single-precision n's result is exactly n's already-narrowed 32-bit float value extended to a double, single precision's own rounding error included and now visible at double precision's wider display.
CHR$(<code>) returns the one-character string whose character code is <code>. <code> must be in 0..255; a value outside that range is "Illegal function call".
CINT(n) returns n rounded to the nearest integer, with ties rounded away from zero. If the rounded result falls outside -32768..32767 it raises Overflow.

Draws a circle, ellipse or arc centred on the given point, which may be absolute or relative to the last point referenced. The radius applies to whichever axis the aspect makes the larger, so an aspect above 1 narrows the horizontal axis rather than lengthening the vertical one. Start and end angles are in radians; a negative angle uses its absolute value and additionally draws a radius line from the centre to that endpoint. Whether a negative start and a negative end each draw their own radius line independently is this interpreter's reading rather than a rule the page states. A trailing F fills the interior: with the palette number written after it, with a tile string, or -- with neither -- in the colour the circle itself was drawn in. With angles present F fills a sector, so the radius lines close the shape even where their angles are positive. A tile string names the pattern an area is filled with instead of a flat colour, and its meaning is defined once, under [2] PAINT (printed p.118-119 / PDF p.129-130) -- CIRCLE's and LINE's entries only refer to it. A tile is always 8 dots wide, and as many rows tall as the string describes: one character makes a row in monochrome mode, three in the 8-colour mode this interpreter targets, four in 16-colour mode. In colour mode the three characters of a row are bit planes rather than three rows -- for each of the eight dot columns the three bits are read downward as a binary number, and that number is the dot's palette, the first character being the 2^0 plane and bit 7 of each byte the leftmost dot. Characters left over at the end of the string, when its length is not a whole number of rows, are ignored; a string too short for even one row is Illegal function call. Where the pattern is anchored is not addressed by the manual: this interpreter repeats it from the screen origin rather than from where a fill starts, so two adjacent fills of one pattern line up, and that reading is ours.

CLEAR [<dummy>][,<memory upper limit>][,<stack size>][,<array data area size>] initializes variables and memory layout. The manual states directly that every numeric variable reverts to 0, every string variable to the null string, and every DEF (DEF FN among them) is invalidated; this interpreter implements exactly that for scalars, arrays (an array reverts to undimensioned, the same state ERASE leaves one in), and DEF FN. OPTION BASE's origin is also put back to unset, since the manual names CLEAR (or RUN) as the only way to change it once fixed. The three numeric slots after the dummy parameter describe memory segment addresses and byte counts this interpreter has no model of -- there is no fixed memory layout to relayout -- so each is parsed and evaluated (a malformed one still reports its own error) and then ignored, which is this interpreter's own reading of "we do not model memory layout" rather than a rule the manual states. The manual does not describe CLEAR interacting with an open FOR/WHILE loop or GOSUB call, or with the DATA cursor, so this interpreter leaves all three untouched -- our own decision, not a stated rule.

CLS [<function>] clears the currently active screen. The function is 1, 2 or 3, and 1 is used when it is left out: 1 clears the text screen only, 2 clears the inside of the graphics viewport, and 3 clears both. Clearing the graphics screen with 2 or 3 paints the viewport in the background colour set by [1] COLOR when SCREEN has put the display in colour mode, and moves the last point referenced to the viewport's top-left corner, so a following LINE with no start point of its own begins there. Clearing the text screen clears within the scroll window CONSOLE has set. This interpreter has no text screen, so CLS 1 -- and therefore a bare CLS -- correctly leaves the graphics framebuffer alone; VIEW is out of scope (spec.md section 3.2), so the viewport CLS 2 and CLS 3 clear is the whole screen and its top-left corner is (0,0). This status is conditional on two facts about other parts of this project, named here so that a change to either trips over them rather than leaving this clause quietly wrong: that there is no text screen (build one and CLS 1 must clear it, so implemented would become partial the same minute), and that VIEW stays out of scope (bring it in and CLS 2 and CLS 3 must clear the viewport rather than the whole screen). Both hold today. The manual does not say what a function code outside 1 to 3 does; this interpreter raises Illegal function call rather than clearing something anyway, and that choice is ours. The text screen is deferred by decision (spec.md SS3.2) rather than merely absent: this interpreter's output is a stream and a text screen is a grid, and the two are different objects. What is unbuilt here is therefore a recorded scope boundary rather than an oversight, and the refusal-free recording of arguments above stays the right behaviour meanwhile.

[1] COLOR takes up to five optional comma-separated arguments: a text-character function code, a background colour, a border colour, a foreground colour, and (DISK mode only) a palette-mode switch; a slot left empty between commas keeps its previous value rather than resetting it. The background and foreground colours are the ones PSET, PRESET and LINE's own omitted-colour arguments fall back to. This interpreter implements the background and foreground slots for that reason; the function code and border are recorded (so a listing setting them still loads and nothing is silently dropped) but have no rasterised effect, since this engine draws no text and no border region at all. The palette-mode slot is refused at run time rather than implemented. The unrelated '=' form the manual calls [2] COLOR, which reassigns what colour a palette number displays, IS implemented now for the 8-of-8 mode -- see SCREEN.COLOR-PALETTE -- so this clause no longer speaks for it. The boundary was an assumption, not a decision, and spec.md SS3.3 now puts palette mode in scope explicitly. The palette-mode slot is therefore an unimplemented feature rather than an omission of this specification, and its refusal stays the right behaviour meanwhile. The mutable palette that [2] COLOR needed has since been built (raster/framebuffer.ml holds palette numbers, resolved at write time), so what remains here is the mode switch itself, not the machinery under it. COLOR@ (printed p.52), a different keyword that colours already-written text-screen characters, is unrelated to COLOR and is not implemented either. The default 8-colour palette's identity, order, and RGB values (raster/palette.ml) are grounded on this same page range: printed p.49 states the order black/blue/red/purple/green/light-blue/yellow/white, and printed p.50's 4096-colour-mode table gives each entry's exact colour code, from which its RGB triple is read. The text screen is deferred by decision (spec.md SS3.2) rather than merely absent: this interpreter's output is a stream and a text screen is a grid, and the two are different objects. What is unbuilt here is therefore a recorded scope boundary rather than an oversight, and the refusal-free recording of arguments above stays the right behaviour meanwhile.

[2] COLOR = (<palette number>, <colour code>) changes which colour a palette number displays. All colour given to the graphics screen is given as a palette number, and this statement is what decides the colour each of those numbers stands for. The palette number names one of the 8 palettes (0-7), or one of 16 (0-15) in the sixteen-colour mode; the colour code says which colour it is to stand for. Which codes are legal depends on the palette mode [1] COLOR selected: the 8-of-8 mode takes the 8 codes 0-7, and both 4096-colour modes take any of &H000 to &HFFF. Any palette number may be given any legal code, and the same code may be given to several palette numbers at once. Writing COLOR with the equals sign and both arguments left off initialises the mapping back to its startup state, which the manual states is valid in DISK mode only. The sixteen-colour mode is honoured only where an analog RGB display is attached; without one it is not an error, the colours simply do not come out as asked. IMPLEMENTED for the 8-of-8 palette mode, which is the only mode this interpreter has, and that includes the indirection itself: reassigning a palette recolours dots ALREADY on the screen. raster/framebuffer.ml stores a palette number per pixel rather than an RGB triple, and the colour each number shows is resolved when the PNG is written, so nothing rewrites a pixel and every pixel drawn through a reassigned palette changes colour at once. The reverse lookup Palette.index_of_rgb that GFX.POINT used to read a pixel back through is gone; POINT now reads the stored palette number directly, and so still reports the palette a dot was drawn THROUGH rather than the colour it currently shows. That retroactive recolouring follows from this page calling the palette the single route by which the graphics screen is given colour, but the page does not say it in as many words. It is stated outright at intro-8801 printed p.119, which walks the reader through it: give palette 0 the colour white, draw a dot specifying colour 0, then give palette 0 the colour blue, and the dot already drawn turns blue. PARTIAL nonetheless, in three respects, each recorded rather than guessed. First, only the 8-of-8 mode exists here, so a colour code is 0-7 and the 4096-colour and sixteen-colour modes are unreachable -- reaching them needs [1] COLOR's palette-mode slot, which is still refused (SCREEN.COLOR). Second, a palette number or colour code outside 0-7 is refused with Illegal function call. That refusal is OURS, not the manual's, which tabulates the legal values and never says what an out-of-range one does; it is refused rather than wrapped so that a listing written for a 4096-colour machine says so instead of silently folding &HF00 to a wrong colour that persists for the rest of the run. It matches this interpreter's existing refusals for an untabulated SCREEN mode, an out-of-range WIDTH and a KEY number outside 1-10. Third, the manual marks the bare initialising form valid in DISK mode only; this interpreter has no such modes, so it is accepted unconditionally, since refusing it would need a mode concept that does not exist here. One further reading is ours: writing the equals sign commits the statement to both arguments, so COLOR= alone and COLOR=(2,) are syntax errors. The page brackets the whole =(<palette>,<code>) group and neither argument within it, but it does not discuss a malformed one. Note also that a COLOR with no arguments at all is this initialising form, while COLOR ,,, is [1] COLOR setting nothing -- the two leave every slot empty and are told apart only by syntax.

CONSOLE [<scroll start line>][,<scroll line count>][,<function key display switch>][,<colour/monochrome switch>] sets the text screen's mode. The first two arguments mark out the scroll window: the region that scrolls runs for <scroll line count> lines from <scroll start line> downward, and it is this window that a text-screen clear -- CLS 1, or PRINT CHR$(12) -- acts on rather than the whole screen. The function key display switch shows the strings defined for the function keys on the bottom line of the screen when it is 1 and stops showing them when it is 0; they are shown immediately after startup. The colour/monochrome switch puts the text screen into colour mode when it is 1 and monochrome when it is 0, and it is monochrome immediately after startup. Every slot is optional and an empty one is written as a bare comma. None of the four has a constant default: an omitted slot leaves that setting as it stands. PARTIAL: this interpreter parses every form and records the four settings in the manual's order, but has no text screen for them to act on, so nothing observes them -- the scroll window in particular bounds a CLS 1 that currently has nothing to clear. The text screen is deferred by decision (spec.md SS3.2) rather than merely absent: this interpreter's output is a stream and a text screen is a grid, and the two are different objects. What is unbuilt here is therefore a recorded scope boundary rather than an oversight, and the refusal-free recording of arguments above stays the right behaviour meanwhile.
COS(n) returns the cosine of n, where n is in radians.

CSNG(n) returns n rounded to single-precision floating point (about 6 significant decimal digits), computed here by round-tripping n through an IEEE-754 32-bit float. If |n| exceeds the manual's stated single-precision bound (1.70141E+38) it raises Overflow.

CSRLIN, always written bare with no parentheses, returns the current text cursor's row, 0 at the top. This interpreter counts newlines the PRINT writer has emitted; it does not reflect LOCATE, which is parsed (SCREEN.LOCATE) but not wired to any cursor state in this interpreter, so a program that repositions the cursor with LOCATE and then reads CSRLIN will not see the effect. That is a gap in this interpreter's screen-state tracking, not a rule the manual states differently, and wiring LOCATE to cursor state is outside what this task's 16 functions cover.

DATA <constant>[,<constant>...] embeds constants in the program for READ to consume. Each constant is either a numeric or a string constant, and expressions are not allowed -- only constants may be written. Constants are separated by commas, and a string constant must be enclosed in double quotes when it contains a comma or a period, when it has leading or embedded spaces that matter, or when it contains two-byte Japanese characters; otherwise the quotes may be left off. A DATA line holds as much data as fits in one line of 255 bytes. A program may contain any number of DATA lines, placed anywhere in it, and READ works through them in ascending line-number order. PARTIAL for one reason, and it is no longer the line limit. That limit -- one line, its number included, within 255 bytes (printed p.9 SS2) -- is enforced by PROG.LINE-LENGTH when the program loads, so it binds a DATA line like any other. Its pattern was widened when this was found. All three forms of an integer constant may be written. Printed p.12 SS5.3 classifies an integer constant into three forms -- octal, decimal and hexadecimal -- and printed p.13 gives them as &O or a bare & for octal and &H for hexadecimal, with its own examples &12345, &O7777, &H100 and &HCFFF. DATA takes constants, so all three belong in it. But DATA items are classified by their own raw-item scanner, separate from the one the rest of a line goes through, and that scanner required a digit after an optional sign. "&HFF" failed the test, was classified as the STRING "&HFF", and only announced itself when a READ tried to take it as a number -- reporting Syntax error on the READ line rather than on the DATA line that held the fault. Every other part of the language read these literals correctly throughout, which is why nothing else showed it. All three forms are accepted now, and a DATA item agrees with the same literal written in an expression. A sign is deliberately NOT part of them: printed p.13 states the sign rule for the decimal form alone, so "-&HFF" stays a string, as do "&HGG" and a bare "&H". What remains partial is the timing of one refusal. On expressions the manual is explicit -- 但し、定数式は使えません, constant expressions cannot be used -- but it fixes neither an error name nor a moment for the rejection, and this interpreter does reject them: 10 DATA 1+2 is accepted where it is written and fails when a READ tries to take it as a number. Deferring the refusal from the DATA line to the READ is therefore a choice of ours about timing, not a rule broken; it is recorded here because the difference is visible to a program that never reads that datum, which runs to completion where the machine would presumably have objected.

DEF FN<name>[(<parameter list>)] = <definition expression> defines a function the program can then call. The name must be a well-formed variable name, and the function may be numeric, string, or a mixture of the two. The parameters name the variables the definition expression uses; they are in effect only while that expression is being evaluated, so a program variable of the same name is untouched by a call and keeps its own value. The parameter list is bracketed in the manual's syntax and may be left off entirely, defining a function of no arguments -- DEF FNA=7 is then called as FNA, with no empty pair of parentheses to write. DEF FN may only be executed from within a program, not as a direct command, which this interpreter satisfies by having no direct mode at all.

DEFDBL <letter>['-'<letter>][,...] declares that every variable or array name starting with a letter in one of the given ranges defaults to double precision, the same way DEFINT declares integer (see PROG.DEFINT for the shared rules on ranges, suffix precedence, and when it takes effect).

DEFINT <letter>['-'<letter>][,...] declares that every variable or array name starting with a letter in one of the given ranges defaults to integer, from that statement onward, unless the name itself carries an explicit type-declaration suffix, which always overrides any DEFxxx declaration (NUM.SUFFIXES). Each range's two letters are inclusive; a single letter with no '-' declares just that one letter. DEFINT may appear anywhere in a program and takes effect for the rest of the run once executed; it is not undone by CLEAR, which the manual describes only as reinitializing values and memory layout, never as reverting a type declaration -- a decision of ours where the manual does not say either way.

DEFSNG <letter>['-'<letter>][,...] declares that every variable or array name starting with a letter in one of the given ranges defaults to single precision, the same way DEFINT declares integer (see PROG.DEFINT for the shared rules). Single precision is already every name's default before any DEFxxx statement runs, so DEFSNG matters only after some other DEFxxx has changed a letter's default and a program wants to set it back.

DEFSTR <letter>['-'<letter>][,...] declares that every variable or array name starting with a letter in one of the given ranges defaults to the string type, the same way DEFINT declares integer (see PROG.DEFINT for the shared rules) -- the one difference being that a name defaulted to string by DEFSTR needs no trailing $ to be treated as a string variable; the letter range alone is enough.
